passage:
Counsellor's note, 22 August.
Uma (Class 10) came in at lunch, which she has never done before. Her class teacher had noticed her eating alone all week. Uma told me that in July she confided in Gurpreet that her parents were separating. Last week a group of girls asked her, in front of everyone, whether it was true her father had "left". She realised Gurpreet had told them.
She said, "I feel so stupid for telling anyone," and that she has stopped talking to all her friends, not only Gurpreet. She kept pulling her sleeves over her hands.
I told her that trusting someone is not stupid, and that the betrayal was not her fault. We agreed she will come on Thursdays for now. With her permission, I will ask her class teacher to change the group-work seating.

qa.q: What did Uma confide in Gurpreet in July?
qa.a: Uma confided that her parents were separating.

qa.q: What does Uma's "I feel so stupid for telling anyone" show?
qa.a: It shows shame and a sense of being exposed, which has led her to pull away from all her friends.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Uma?
qa.a: The counsellor said trusting wasn't stupid or her fault, set up Thursday meetings, and, with her permission, planned to ask about changing the seating.

qa.q: What would change if Gurpreet had kept the confidence?
qa.a: Uma would still have someone to lean on during her parents' separation, instead of eating alone and guarding herself with everyone.

grounding: A counsellor records how a teenage girl, finding that a confidant told others her family news, feels exposed and withdraws from everyone.

passage:
Friday, 11 pm.
I told exactly one person that I write songs. Imran. On the terrace last month I even sang him half of one. He said it was really good and that he wouldn't tell anyone.
Today in music class, Sir said, "I hear Vandana is a secret songwriter! Come, sing us something." Everyone turned. I said I had a sore throat. My face was on fire. At the back, Imran gave me a thumbs-up, like it was a present.
Maybe he thought he was helping. I don't care. It was MINE to share.
I'm not telling anyone anything again. Not Imran, not anyone in my class. It's safer to keep everything in here.
V.

qa.q: What did Vandana tell Imran on the terrace?
qa.a: Vandana told Imran about writing songs and sang him half of one.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when Sir announced the secret?
qa.a: Vandana felt exposed and embarrassed; the face was on fire and a sore throat became the excuse not to sing.

qa.q: What could Vandana try instead of shutting everyone out?
qa.a: Vandana could tell Imran calmly why it hurt, so he learns the difference between cheering someone on and sharing their private news.

qa.q: Why might Imran have told the music teacher?
qa.a: He may have thought he was helping, as his thumbs-up suggests, without realising the news was Vandana's to share.

grounding: A teenager finds a confidant told the teacher about private songwriting, feels exposed and foolish, and decides to guard everything from now on.

passage:
At the bus stand of the small town, the school girls waited in the shade of the peepal tree. When Reena walked up, the talking stopped.
Then one of them said, sweetly, "Reena, is it true your father lost his job at the mill?"
Reena's face went hot. She had told only one person: Sonali, sitting beside her on the wall last Sunday, sharing a packet of chana.
She looked at Sonali now. Sonali was staring at her own shoes.
Reena said nothing. When the bus came, she sat alone at the front instead of in their usual seat at the back. At lunch, she ate her roti behind the library.
For the next week, when her Dadi asked how school was, she said, "Fine." When Sonali tried to talk, Reena answered in single words. She began to feel safer keeping everything to herself.

qa.q: Where had Reena told Sonali about her father?
qa.a: Sitting beside her on the wall last Sunday, sharing a packet of chana.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when the girl asked about her father's job?
qa.a: Reena felt exposed and ashamed, her face going hot, because a private family matter had been shared.

qa.q: What could Sonali do to try to repair things?
qa.a: Sonali could apologise to Reena privately, own what she did, and ask the other girls to stop talking about it.

qa.q: How does Sonali seem to feel when Reena looks at her?
qa.a: Sonali seems guilty, which is why she stares at her own shoes.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning a confidant shared a family secret, feeling exposed and foolish, and becoming more guarded with everyone.

passage:
At the summer camp near Guadalajara, Javier had told only Ivan the truth on the first night, whispering from the top bunk: he couldn't swim. Not even a little. He had pretended to have an ear infection to skip the pool.
On Thursday, before the lake trip, a boy from another cabin shouted across the dining hall, "Hey, Javier! Want some arm floats?" The whole table laughed.
Javier looked at Ivan. Ivan's face went red. "I only told Marco," he muttered. "I didn't think…"
Javier pushed his tray away. He felt stupid, as if everyone could see straight through him.
That afternoon he stayed in the cabin, reading. When Ivan came back and said sorry, Javier nodded but didn't look up.
On the last night, the others told ghost stories and secrets. Javier lay on his bunk and said nothing at all.

qa.q: What did Javier tell Ivan on the first night?
qa.a: He told him he couldn't swim.

qa.q: How did Javier feel when the boy shouted about arm floats?
qa.a: Javier felt humiliated and foolish, as if everyone could see straight through him.

qa.q: What could Ivan do to repair the trust?
qa.a: Ivan could own it without excuses, ask Marco and the others to stop the jokes, and stand with Javier in front of them.

qa.q: What is it like for Ivan when Javier won't look up?
qa.a: Ivan feels guilty and shut out, realising his slip has cost him his friend's trust.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning a confidant spread his secret, feeling exposed and withdrawing, more guarded with everyone after.

passage:
In the girls' hostel of the residential school in Ooty, Lakshmi heard it from the next cubicle: "Lakshmi likes Pranav from 11B. Sachin told everyone at football."
She stood very still behind the door. She had told only one person, Sachin, her friend since Class 6, in the library last week, because he'd asked why she kept going red.
By dinner three boys hummed a love song when she passed. She laughed it off. In the dorm she pulled the blanket over her head.
For the next week she stopped sitting with Sachin at study hour. She stopped sitting with anyone. When her roommate asked what she was reading, she said, "Nothing," and turned the page.
On Friday the house mother, Mrs Joseph, found her alone on the steps. "You've gone very quiet this week. Did something happen?"
Lakshmi shrugged. Then, slowly, she told her.

qa.q: Where had Lakshmi told Sachin her secret?
qa.a: In the library last week.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after hearing the girls in the next cubicle?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt exposed and foolish, standing very still and later hiding under the blanket.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi start to open up again?
qa.a: Mrs Joseph noticing she'd gone quiet and asking gently, which gave Lakshmi a safe person to tell.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the change in Lakshmi?
qa.a: Sachin would see his friend since Class 6 stop sitting with him, and might realise how much sharing her secret hurt.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning a friend shared her secret, feeling exposed and foolish, and withdrawing from everyone afterwards.
